subject: Vocabulary
topic: Common English Idioms — Meaning and Usage

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'Bite the bullet' mean?

options.option_text: To be extremely hungry
To endure a painful or difficult situation with courage
To deliberately lie or mislead someone
To attack someone unexpectedly

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Bite the bullet' = to endure a painful, difficult, or unpleasant situation stoically, without complaining. Origin: soldiers in battle would bite on a bullet during battlefield surgery (before anaesthesia) to cope with pain. 'She decided to bite the bullet and accept the pay cut.'

questions.stem: What is the meaning of 'Burn the midnight oil'?

options.option_text: To waste energy on unnecessary tasks
To work or study late into the night
To destroy important documents secretly
To be extremely angry about something

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Burn the midnight oil' = to stay up very late working or studying. Before electric lights, students would burn oil lamps late at night to continue working. 'She had to burn the midnight oil to finish the project before the deadline.'

questions.stem: What does 'Let the cat out of the bag' mean?

options.option_text: To release an animal in a wild area
To reveal a secret accidentally
To start a quarrel or fight suddenly
To give someone permission to proceed

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Let the cat out of the bag' = to accidentally or prematurely reveal a secret. 'He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party when he mentioned it to the guests.' This is one of the most tested idioms in SSC/bank exams.

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of 'Hit the nail on the head':

options.option_text: To make a carpentry error
To accomplish something with great difficulty
To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem
To punish someone harshly for a mistake

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Hit the nail on the head' = to say or identify something exactly right; to be precisely accurate in describing a problem or situation. 'When she said the new policy would hurt small businesses, she really hit the nail on the head.' Reference to driving a nail perfectly with a hammer.

Being neutral or undecided between two choices
Being trapped in a difficult situation with no escape
Making a risky investment decision

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'On the fence' = being neutral; not committed to either side of an argument or decision; undecided. 'The senator was on the fence about the new tax legislation.' Visual: literally sitting on a fence between two sides, unable to choose which side to land on.

options.option_text: To punch a punching bag
To fire or dismiss an employee
To go to bed and sleep
To leave a place suddenly and without notice

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Hit the sack' = to go to bed; to go to sleep. 'I'm exhausted — I'm going to hit the sack early tonight.' 'Sack' is informal for a bed. Exam trap: 'get the sack/give someone the sack' = to be fired from a job — completely different idiom.

questions.stem: The idiom 'Under the weather' most closely means:

options.option_text: In a dangerous outdoor situation
Feeling ill or unwell
Facing financial difficulties
Being confused or disoriented

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Under the weather' = feeling ill, sick, or not in good health. 'She called in sick today — she's been feeling a bit under the weather.' Origin: sailors who were sick would go below deck (under the weather deck) to avoid rough weather.

questions.stem: What is the meaning of 'A blessing in disguise'?

options.option_text: A hidden danger that appears harmless
Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
A prayer said in secret without others knowing
Receiving an unexpected monetary gift

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'A blessing in disguise' = something that initially appears bad but ultimately turns out to be beneficial. 'Losing that job was a blessing in disguise — he found a much better one the following month.' A core idiom in all bank/SSC/railway exam vocabularies.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'Beat around the bush' mean?

options.option_text: To search for something hidden in a difficult location
To avoid coming to the main point; to talk around an issue
To win a competition through unconventional tactics
To punish someone using extreme measures

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Beat around the bush' = to avoid talking about what is important; to talk about minor things instead of addressing the main issue. 'Stop beating around the bush and tell me the reason for your visit.' Origin: hunters beating surrounding bushes to flush out game birds, approaching the main point (bush) indirectly.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the idiom 'Go back to the drawing board'?

options.option_text: After the accident, the artist went back to the drawing board to sketch new designs.
The new product launch failed, so the team had to go back to the drawing board and redesign the strategy.
She went back to the drawing board to retrieve her sketchbook.
He returned to the drawing board to correct a minor detail in his plan.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Go back to the drawing board' = to start again from the beginning, usually after a plan has failed. A 'drawing board' is where architects and engineers draft plans; going back means scrapping the current plan and starting fresh. 'The bridge design collapsed under testing — the engineers had to go back to the drawing board.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of 'Throw in the towel':

options.option_text: To start a new competition or challenge
To surrender or give up on a task or contest
To make a dramatic entrance into a situation
To clean up after completing a task

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Throw in the towel' = to admit defeat; to stop trying. Origin: boxing — a trainer would throw a towel into the ring to signal that their fighter is giving up. 'After three failed attempts to pass the exam, he finally threw in the towel.' Synonyms: 'give up', 'call it quits', 'raise the white flag'.
